history.note: baseline probe of the mid-range geometry
history.thinking:
Baseline probe. No evidence yet, so no intent: this iteration only
establishes where the notch naturally falls for the mid-range starting
geometry (ro=8mm, alpha=90deg, ri=0.3mm, Wf=0.6mm, Lc=3mm). A radial stub
behaves as a quarter-wave shunt resonator whose resonant frequency scales
roughly as 1/ro, so the measured notch frequency here tells me which
direction ro has to move and by how much.

history.note: notch at 3.30 GHz is 1.67x too low; shrink ro hard
history.thinking:
Evidence: the resonator is healthy but mistuned. The sweep already shows a
very deep notch (-50.3 dB) at 3.300 GHz, so the butterfly does short the
through path properly -- it just does it at the wrong frequency. At the
frequency I actually care about, 5.5 GHz, I am only getting -11.1 dB.

Diagnosis: I need to move the resonance up by a factor 5.5/3.3 = 1.67.
For a radial stub the resonant length is set mainly by the fan radius, and
resonant frequency scales roughly as 1/ro, so ro wants to go from 8 mm to
somewhere near 4.8 mm. That is a big move -- about 29% of the full ro range
[3, 14] -- so this is clearly a "strong" step, not a nudge.

I am touching ro only. ri, alpha, Wf and Lc all perturb the resonance too,
but far more weakly, and changing several variables at once on the very
first move would make the response impossible to attribute. Coarse tuning
first with the single dominant variable, fine tuning with the rest later.

history.note: fit f=21.6/(ro-1.45) wants ro=5.38; slight step undershoots less than a normal one
history.thinking:
The strong move worked and it gave me something better than a direction: it
gave me a calibration. Two points now relate fan radius to notch frequency,
ro=8.000 -> 3.300 GHz and ro=5.954 -> 4.800 GHz, and the cost at 5.5 GHz
improved from -11.1 dB to -20.2 dB.

Note that f*ro is not constant (26.4 vs 28.6), so the pure 1/ro model is
wrong. Fitting f = k/(ro + c) against the two points gives c = -1.45 and
k = 21.6, i.e. the electrical length has a fixed offset from the feed, the
inner radius and the cross junction that does not scale with ro. Solving
that fit for 5.5 GHz asks for ro = 5.38 mm, so I want a delta of about
-0.57 mm.

The step ladder at iteration 2 (decay 0.93^2) offers -0.38 mm for "slight"
and -0.95 mm for "normal". Neither is exact. I take the slight one: it
leaves me at ro = 5.57 predicting 5.24 GHz, an undershoot of 0.26 GHz,
whereas the normal step would overshoot to 6.09 GHz and be 0.59 GHz off.
Approaching the target from one side also keeps my fit valid instead of
throwing me across the resonance where I would have to re-learn the slope.

df/dro = -1.34 GHz per mm, and the smallest ro step this schedule will ever

finish this job. After this move I stop steering with ro and start probing
alpha, Wf and ri one at a time to measure their frequency sensitivities --
their ranges are far narrower, so their smallest steps are the fine
adjustment I will need at the end.

history.note: ro is out of resolution; probe alpha sensitivity, expecting notch down
history.thinking:
Target is now bracketed: ro = 5.573 put the notch at 5.200 GHz, ro = 5.220
puts it at 5.700 GHz, and cost keeps improving (-31.8 dB). The local slope
across that bracket is df/dro = -1.42 GHz/mm, so closing the remaining
-0.200 GHz needs ro to grow by only +0.141 mm.

The smallest ro step on offer at iteration 4 is +0.329 mm, which would
overshoot to roughly 5.23 GHz -- worse than where I already am. This is the
resolution wall I predicted one step ago, and it confirms ro is finished as
a steering variable. Continuing to bounce it up and down would just cycle
between 5.2 and 5.7 GHz forever, which is exactly the trap I want to avoid.

So I switch modes: from steering to probing. I spend this iteration
measuring the frequency sensitivity of alpha, because alpha's range is
[30, 150] deg and a slight step is 3.59 deg -- small in relative terms, and
its step will keep shrinking as the schedule decays, giving me the fine
control ro cannot.

Direction: I need the notch to come DOWN 0.2 GHz. Widening the sector adds
metal and capacitive loading to the fan, which should lengthen it
electrically and lower the resonance, so I go increase_slight. If the notch
instead moves up, the probe is still a success -- I will have learned the
sign, and I invert it next iteration.

history.note: alpha is the fine/depth knob; probe ri as the mid-resolution frequency knob
history.thinking:
This probe returned something far more valuable than the sensitivity number
I asked for. Widening alpha by 3.59 deg did NOT move the notch off the
5.700 GHz grid point -- but its depth collapsed from -50.5 dB to -84.9 dB.
The cost at 5.5 GHz barely moved (-31.8 -> -31.3 dB), so in isolation this
looks like a wasted step. It is not.

Two readings fit that observation, and both are good news. Either alpha
controls the notch depth directly by balancing the shunt branch into a truer
short, or -- more likely given how sharp this resonance is -- alpha nudged
the notch centre by only a few MHz, just enough to land it almost exactly on
the 5.700 GHz sample instead of beside it. A -84.9 dB reading on a 50 MHz
grid means the true centre is essentially on that grid point.

Either way the conclusion is the same and it is the one I needed: alpha is
the fine knob and ro is the coarse knob. The machine can already produce a
notch far deeper than the -70 dB goal; the entire remaining problem is
sliding that notch 200 MHz down onto 5.5 GHz without wrecking its depth.

Next I need a frequency knob with resolution between ro's 0.31 mm (about
440 MHz) and alpha's near-zero. ri is the candidate: the fan's radiating
length is ro - ri, so growing ri shortens it and raises the resonance, and
shrinking ri should lower it. I want the notch lower, so I probe with
decrease at normal magnitude, -0.097 mm. If ri really is as sensitive as ro
in per-mm terms, that is about -0.14 GHz and lands me near 5.56 GHz. This
probe measures the sensitivity and moves me toward the target at the same
time, which is strictly better than a probe that only measures.

The probe answered clearly, and my physical guess about magnitude was wrong
in a useful way. ri went 0.300 -> 0.203, a change of -0.097 mm, and the

knew the slope. What I bought is the complete sensitivity map:

  ri     5.68 GHz/mm, range 1.4  -> smallest step at iter 6 is 0.21 GHz
  ro     1.42 GHz/mm, range 11   -> smallest step at iter 6 is 0.40 GHz
  alpha  under 0.05 GHz per 3.6 deg -- below the sweep grid, the sub-grid trimmer

Now the arithmetic. I sit at 5.150 GHz and need +0.350 GHz. The slight ro
step is -0.285 mm, worth +0.404 GHz, landing at 5.554 -- an error of only
+0.054 GHz. The slight ri step is worth +0.206 GHz, landing at 5.356, an
error of -0.144 GHz. ro wins this round, which is a nice reversal: the
coarse variable is the accurate one here purely because its step happens to
match the gap.

Note that ro decreasing raises frequency, so "closer to target" means
decrease_slight even though I am moving upward in frequency.

history.note: alpha sets notch floor not frequency; gradient says go down, step past iter-6 alpha
history.thinking:
Wrong sign. Widening alpha by 2.89 deg made everything slightly worse: cost
-43.1 -> -41.1 dB, and the depth read at 5.550 GHz also fell, -61.1 ->
-58.5 dB. Both samples degrading at once is the interesting part, so I
checked it properly instead of assuming.

If the notch were a clean transmission zero, |S21| would grow linearly with
detuning near the centre, and the ratio of the two samples locates that
centre. At iteration 6 the ratio 0.007003/0.000884 puts the centre at
5.5447 GHz; at iteration 7 the ratio 0.008825/0.001190 puts it at
5.5443 GHz. The centre did not move -- it shifted by under half a MHz --
yet both readings got worse.

So my earlier reading of the iteration-4 probe was the wrong one of the two.
alpha is not a fine frequency trimmer. alpha controls how perfectly the
shunt branch realises the zero: it sets the floor of the notch, not its
position. That also explains iteration 4 cleanly -- -84.9 dB there was a
near-perfect zero, not a lucky grid alignment.

That reframes the endgame usefully. The notch centre is parked at 5.544 GHz
and needs -44 MHz, which is still finer than any ro or ri step. But depth
and frequency are now decoupled knobs, so I can drive them separately
instead of hoping one move fixes both.

Depth first, because the gradient is unambiguous and cheap: 96.5 deg is
worse than 93.6 deg, so alpha goes down. I take a normal step, -6.72 deg to
89.76 deg. That is 2.3x the move I just measured and pushes past the best
alpha I have seen rather than merely undoing this step, which would waste
the iteration re-measuring a point I already have.

history.note: three-point alpha trend is monotone and steepening; keep descending
history.thinking:
Best cost so far, -46.98 dB, and the shape of the response changed in a way
worth reading carefully. The two samples either side are now almost equal --
0.004478 at 5.500 and 0.003767 at 5.550, where at iteration 6 they differed
by a factor of eight. Feeding that ratio through the same centre estimate
puts the notch at 5.527 GHz, down from 5.545.

So my last conclusion was too absolute. alpha is not purely a depth knob: it
moves the centre too, at roughly 4.6 MHz per degree, which is exactly the
fine frequency resolution I was hunting for. What confused me at iteration 7
was that the linear-zero centre estimate only holds while the notch is deep;
at iteration 7 the floor had risen enough to bias it, and I read "no
frequency shift" out of what was really "estimator broke". Worth remembering
that the estimate is only trustworthy when the two samples differ a lot.

The honest, model-free summary is the one I should act on. Cost at 5.5 GHz
against alpha reads 96.48 deg -> -41.1 dB, 93.59 deg -> -43.1 dB, 89.76 deg
-> -47.0 dB. Three points, monotone, and steepening. I have not passed the
optimum yet.

The floor did get worse in absolute terms -- the deepest point in the sweep
went from -61.1 to -48.5 dB -- but that is the wrong thing to optimise. I am
not paid for a deep notch somewhere, I am paid for depth at 5.5 GHz exactly,
and the centre marching toward 5.5 is worth more than the floor rising.

Another normal step down, -6.25 deg to 83.52 deg. Same magnitude class that
just earned 3.9 dB, and the decay schedule is shrinking it for me anyway, so
I do not need to hedge manually yet.

history.note: goal met at -84.2 dB; bracket test to check whether 83.5 deg is the optimum
history.thinking:
Goal met, and by a wide margin: -84.23 dB at 5.500 GHz against a -70 dB
target. The deepest point in the entire 1-10 GHz sweep is now the 5.500 GHz
sample itself, which is the cleanest possible confirmation that the notch
centre landed on the target rather than near it.

The jump was -47.0 -> -84.2 dB from a single 6.25 deg move, which looks
violent until you remember what the cost function is. |S21| at a fixed
frequency near a transmission zero is roughly linear in the detuning, so as
the centre crosses the sample point the dB reading falls off a cliff. The
last three alpha values walked the centre from 5.545 to 5.527 to essentially
5.500 GHz -- a steady 4-5 MHz per degree the whole way. The cost curve looked
"steepening" only because I was watching a linear quantity through a log.

I could stop here. I am not going to, for one reason: I do not know whether
I stopped on the optimum or merely inside the pit, and one cheap step settles
it. State is checkpointed and `best` tracks the minimum, so a worse result
costs nothing but the iteration.

alpha decrease_slight, -2.32 deg to 81.20. This is a bracket test, not a
descent step. If the cost improves, the optimum is below 81.2 and I keep
going. If it degrades, the optimum is bracketed between 81.20 and 89.76 with
83.52 the best sample, and I stop rather than grind at a notch already 14 dB
past spec.

history.thinking:
The bracket closed. alpha = 81.20 deg gives -55.5 dB, clearly worse than
83.52 deg's -84.2 dB, so the optimum lies between 81.20 and 89.76 and I have
walked past it rather than stalled short of it.

Three samples is enough to locate it properly instead of guessing. Near a
transmission zero |S21| is linear in the detuning, and alpha maps linearly
onto centre frequency, so |S21| should be roughly A*|alpha - alpha_star|.
Taking the ratio of the 81.196 and 83.519 samples gives alpha_star = 83.61
deg and A = 6.9e-4 per degree. The real test is that this fit was built
without the 89.764 point and then predicts it: it says |S21| = 0.00427
there, and the simulator measured 0.004478. Within 5%. The model is sound.

That number also tells me to stop, which is the useful part. From where I
now stand at 81.196 deg the ladder offers +2.16 deg (slight) or +5.40 deg
(normal) at iteration 11. Slight lands at 83.357, which is 0.25 deg short of
alpha_star and predicts -75.2 dB; normal lands at 86.60 and predicts about
-53.7 dB. Iteration 9's 83.519 deg sits only 0.088 deg from the optimum, and
no step available from here gets closer. Waiting for the decay to shrink the
step does not help either, because by iteration 12 the slight step has only
fallen to 2.01 deg and still lands short.

So I take the slight step as a falsification test rather than an improvement
attempt. My model says -75.2 dB. If the simulator agrees within a decibel or
so, the quantitative picture I built over the last five iterations is
verified, iteration 9 stands as the answer, and I stop with a reason instead
of running out of budget. If it comes back far off, the model is wrong and
the remaining nine iterations are worth spending.

conclusion:
My model was wrong, and the way it was wrong is the most useful thing this
run produced. I predicted -75.2 dB at alpha = 83.356 deg and the simulator
returned -84.62 dB -- off by 9.4 dB, and better than the iteration 9 result
I was trying to confirm. The falsification test falsified the model rather
than the design.

What went wrong is that I fitted the zero location using the 81.196 and
83.519 samples, one on each side, and assumed the V is symmetric. It is not:
refitting on all six samples taken at this ro/ri/Wf/Lc slice --

  81.196 -> 0.001683      83.356 -> 0.000059
  83.519 -> 0.000061      89.764 -> 0.004478
  93.591 -> 0.007003      96.479 -> 0.008825

-- puts the zero at alpha_star = 83.44 deg with a noticeably steeper slope on
the low side (about 9.4e-4 per degree) than the high side (about 6.6e-4).
The single-sided fit that predicted the 89.764 point to within 5% simply does
not extrapolate across the vertex.

This is where the run ends, and not because the goal is met. It ends because
the search has hit the resolution floor of its own step ladder. The two best
samples, 83.356 and 83.519 deg, straddle alpha_star at about 0.08 deg each.
The smallest alpha step the intent schedule can ever emit is a slight step at
the decay floor, 0.04 x 0.15 x 120 = 0.72 deg -- nine times larger than the
distance I still have to travel. At iteration 12 the actual slight step is
2.01 deg, which would land at 85.37 deg and cost about 27 dB. Every remaining
move in every remaining iteration overshoots. No sequence of them converges.

Final state: -84.62 dB at 5.500 GHz, 14.6 dB past the -70 dB goal, reached in
11 iterations against the demo run's 17 to reach -70.3 dB. The deepest point
in the whole 1-10 GHz sweep is the 5.500 GHz sample itself.

The honest caveat is that the passband is now poor -- mean |S21| is 0.75
below 4 GHz and 0.26 above 6 GHz, and it degraded steadily while I drove the
notch down. Nothing in total_cost penalises that, so the optimizer was never
asked to care. If this design has to be usable rather than just deep, the
cost function needs a passband term before the next run, not a smarter
strategy layer.

If someone wants to push past -84.62 dB, the fix is in intent.py, not here:
either add an "increase_fine"/"decrease_fine" magnitude below "slight", or
lower the _MIN_SCALE floor so late iterations can emit sub-0.1 deg steps.
That is a change to the arithmetic layer, which is exactly where it belongs
-- the strategy layer should not be the thing inventing smaller numbers.
